q: 281. In concrete walls, construction joints should be provided at the
explain: Construction joints in concrete walls can be located at floor level, soffit level, or sill level depending on the pour sequence — all of these are acceptable locations.

q: 282. The construction joints on cement concrete
options: should be located where bending moment is large
should be located where shear force is large
should not be provided at the corners
should be spaced at a distance of 3 m apart in case of huge structures
explain: Construction joints should specifically be avoided at corners of structures, as these are critical stress locations prone to cracking.

q: 283. The increase in strength of concrete after 6 months
explain: As per the strength-gain data referenced in this text, concrete strength increases by about 20% beyond the 28-day value after 6 months of curing.

q: 284. The drying of concrete after casting results in
explain: As moisture evaporates from freshly cast concrete, the paste loses volume, causing drying shrinkage.

q: 285. The type of cement preferred in the construction of massive concrete dam is
explain: Low heat cement is preferred for massive dam construction because it minimizes the heat of hydration, reducing the risk of thermal cracking in large concrete masses.

q: 286. As per IS specifications, full strength of concrete is attained ......... days after casting.
explain: As per standard IS convention, the full/characteristic strength of concrete is considered to be attained at 28 days after casting.

q: 287. Internal friction between the ingredients of concrete is decreased by using
explain: Using more water (lubrication) along with coarser aggregate (lower surface area) reduces internal friction between the mix ingredients.

q: 288. High temperature
options: has no effect on strength of concrete
explain: High placing/curing temperature accelerates early hydration but leads to a weaker, more porous concrete matrix, ultimately decreasing its long-term strength.

q: 289. Placing of concrete should probably be done at a temperature of
explain: As per the recommended condition in this text, concrete placing should ideally be done at a temperature of about 27 ± 2°C for proper hydration and finishing behavior.

q: 290. Water required per bag of cement is
explain: As a general rule referenced in this text, about 28 kg (litres) of water is required per 50 kg bag of cement for a typical nominal mix.

q: 291. CRRI charts are used to obtain relationship between strength of concrete and
explain: CRRI (Central Road Research Institute) charts are specifically used to establish the relationship between concrete strength and water-cement ratio for mix design purposes.

q: 292. Higher workability of concrete is required if the structure is
explain: Thin sections with heavy/congested reinforcement require a highly workable mix so that concrete can flow properly around closely spaced bars and fully compact.

q: 293. For ensuring quality of concrete, use
explain: Using well-graded aggregate (a proper mix of different particle sizes) ensures minimum voids, better packing, and consequently higher-quality, denser concrete.

q: 294. To determine modulus of rupture, the size of test specimen used is
explain: As per IS 516, the standard flexural (modulus of rupture) test beam specimen size is 150 × 150 × 700 mm.

q: 295. Workability of concrete is directly proportional to
explain: Well-graded aggregate reduces void content and improves the flow characteristics of the mix, thereby directly improving workability.

q: 296. Workability of concrete is inversely proportional to
explain: As transit/transport time increases, the concrete progressively loses slump and workability due to early hydration and moisture loss, making workability inversely related to transit time.

q: 297. Approximate value of shrinkage strain in concrete
explain: The typical order of magnitude for drying shrinkage strain in ordinary concrete is about 0.0003 (i.e., 3×10⁻⁴).

q: 298. Air entraining in the concrete increases
explain: Entrained air bubbles act as tiny ball bearings within the mix, improving the flow and workability of fresh concrete.

q: 299. The relation between modulus of rupture fcr, splitting strength fcs, and direct tensile strength fq is given by
explain: Among the different tensile strength measures of concrete, the flexural (modulus of rupture) value is the highest, followed by the split cylinder strength, with the direct tensile strength being the lowest: fcr > fcs > fct.

q: 300. The approximate value of the ratio between direct tensile strength and flexural strength is
explain: As given in this text, the direct tensile strength of concrete is approximately half (0.5 times) its flexural strength (modulus of rupture).
